sections.overview: The straw-coloured fruit bat is one of the largest fruit bats of Africa and the most widespread. It roosts in very large colonies, makes long migrations and is listed as Near Threatened.
sections.identification: A large bat with a body of about 14–21 cm and a weight of 230–350 g, males being slightly bigger. The neck and back are straw-coloured and the underside a duller brown or grey. The wings are long and narrow, built for long flights, and the head is large and pointed with big eyes and no white facial markings. Wingspan is given as up to about 75 cm in one source and up to one metre in another.
sections.habitat: It lives across most of sub-Saharan Africa and in the south-west of the Arabian Peninsula, in forest and savanna from coastal forest to dry regions, and from sea level to about 2,000 m. Tropical forest is its prime habitat because of the abundant food. It roosts mainly in tall trees and sometimes in caves, and also uses towns and farmland.
sections.diet: It sucks the juice from fruit and spits out the pulp. Reported foods include mangoes, dates, figs, pawpaws and avocados, as well as the flowers of baobab, Borassus palms and silk-cotton trees. It also chews soft wood and bark, apparently for moisture. It feeds in the open upper canopy and can eat a large quantity in a night.
sections.behavior: It is social and nocturnal: colonies rest in trees by day and leave the roost at night in small groups, flying in straight lines and at greater heights than other fruit bats. It forages up to about 30 km from the roost and is noisy, chattering in the roost and while eating. It is a long-distance migrant: every year millions gather at Kasanka National Park in Zambia, and it holds the longest migration recorded for an African mammal.
sections.reproduction: It breeds once a year, with mating from April to June, and most populations show delayed implantation, so that births come in February and March. A single young of about 50 g is usual; it cannot fly at birth and only the female cares for it. The sources disagree on the total length of gestation (nine months or about 275 days).
sections.ecology: By visiting flowers it pollinates trees of the mulberry and silk-cotton families, and by carrying fruit it disperses seeds. Owls, eagles, buzzards, snakes and civets prey on it, and it is eaten by people in parts of West and Central Africa. Where colonies roost near orchards it can be a crop pest.
sections.conservation: It is listed as Near Threatened. Bushmeat hunting is a main cause of local declines in West and Central Africa, and deforestation is the greatest threat overall. In some areas bats are seen as pests and their roosts are destroyed. Reports of colony size vary widely, from tens of thousands to millions, and one source calls the species very abundant.
